cover: THE CDC SAYS: DON'T WASH RAW CHICKEN.
THE USDA SAYS WASHING CAN SPLASH GERMS
MOST OF US DO IT EVERY WEEK.

slides.text: Rinse the chicken. Pat it dry. Into the pan. It feels clean. It feels like what a careful cook does.
Water carries bacteria off raw chicken and into a 2 to 3 foot splash zone: your counter, your sponge, your salad.
After people washed raw poultry, 60% had bacteria in the sink. About 1 in 4 moved it onto lettuce nearby.
Skip the rinse. Pat it dry with a paper towel. Cook it all the way to 165°F. Heat kills the germs. Washing doesn't.
I'd trusted a habit for 30 years because nobody ever told me. What else am I doing out of habit?

cta_hook: The habit felt careful. It wasn't.
cta_bridge: We read every label. Nobody reads what their body is telling them.
caption:
My mother rinsed her chicken in the sink until the day she died. She called it "being careful."

I did it too for thirty years. Then a food safety class changed what I do in my kitchen.

Here's what the CDC and USDA say, in plain words.

1. Washing spreads it
Water splashes bacteria like Salmonella off raw chicken, and the USDA says it can land in a 2 to 3 foot radius: your counter, your dish towel, the sponge, a salad bowl.

2. Their own test
In a USDA study, 60% of people who washed raw poultry had bacteria in the sink afterward. About a quarter transferred it to lettuce sitting nearby.

3. What works instead
Don't rinse. Pat dry with a paper towel. Cook to 165°F, which kills the germs. Then wipe your counter with hot soapy water and sanitize it.

When I told my sister, she said, "But that's how Mom taught us." Exactly. Nobody ever questioned it.

I stood in my kitchen holding a wet piece of chicken, and I realized I'd been doing something for thirty years because no one asked why.

I don't think I'm the only one running on habits I never checked.

One more tip from the same class: use separate cutting boards for raw meat and vegetables, and wash your hands for 20 seconds with soap after touching raw chicken. Small changes, no special equipment, and they cost nothing.

We check labels, bills and fine print. I started reading what my body had been trying to tell me, and put it in one place: four short books (The Belly Fat Lie, Aging Faster Than You Should, The Caffeine Trap, The 3AM Signal) and four tools. That's the Health Bundle.

cover: PAY $100 A MONTH ON $5,000 OF CARD DEBT AT 22%
YOUR STATEMENT HAS TO SHOW YOU THIS NUMBER:

slides.text: $5,000 on a card at 22% interest. You pay $100 a month. Feels responsible. It takes 11 years and costs about $13,700.
slides.loop: Most of it isn't your debt.

slides.text: Early on, most of every payment is interest. The balance barely drops for months. That's how it works by design.
By law, your statement must show how many months it takes to pay off the balance if you pay only the minimum.
It must also show the monthly payment that clears the balance in 3 years. For this card, about $191 a month.
I'd read every line of my statement except the one box. I made a plan for my money. Not for my body.

cta_hook: A plan for your money. A plan for your body.
cta_bridge: I invested in everything except the one thing I can't replace.
caption:
The number she'd never seen was printed on her statement every month. She just never read that box.

My friend Beth was paying $100 a month toward a $5,000 balance. She felt proud of it. She was also quietly stressed about the same card.

We sat down with her statement and a calculator.

1. The real math
$5,000 at 22% APR, paying $100 a month: about 137 payments. That's over 11 years and roughly $13,700 total. Most of it is interest.

2. The box on your statement
Under the CARD Act, your statement must show how many months it takes to pay the balance off at the minimum payment, and what monthly payment clears it in 3 years.

3. The 3-year number
For her balance, about $191 a month. Beth cut one subscription and one dinner out and found the money in a week.

She paid it off in three years.

When she told her brother, he said, "At your age, who cares about a credit card?" Beth said, "At my age, I'd like the last decade of my life to be mine."

Money is a plan. The same goes for your health. Beth said the scariest part of her statement wasn't the number. It was how long she'd looked at that page without reading it.

She taped the page to her fridge with the two numbers circled. Her husband said it was the first time he'd seen the whole picture. Sometimes the answer is already in the mail, in a box nobody reads.

I planned my money for decades and never planned for my body. This is the plan I wish I'd had at 40, and I put it in one place: four short books (The Belly Fat Lie, Aging Faster Than You Should, The Caffeine Trap, The 3AM Signal) and four tools. That's the Health Bundle.

cover: "ASK FOR ANGELA" IS A SAFETY CODE USED IN BARS
ACROSS THE UK, IRELAND AND CANADA.

slides.text: You're on a bad date, or someone won't leave you alone. You walk to the bar and ask: "Is Angela working tonight?"
Trained staff can walk you to a safe area, call a cab, help you reach a friend, or ask the other person to leave.
It began in Lincolnshire, England, in 2016, as a campaign backed by local police. It spread to Ireland and Canada.
It only works where venues are trained. Look for a poster or ask before you need it. I couldn't confirm US venues.
A secret phrase only works if someone has agreed to listen. What do I do when my body asks for help?

cta_hook: Some signals only work if someone's listening.
cta_bridge: I learned to read every warning sign except the ones my body sends.
caption:
The bartender never looked at her. That was the whole point.

My niece told me about a night out that went wrong. A man wouldn't take no for an answer. She remembered a poster in the restroom and asked the bartender one sentence: "Is Angela working tonight?"

Here's how "Ask for Angela" works, based on police and local council pages.

1. The request
You ask a bartender, bouncer or staff member: "Is Angela working?" It's a quiet signal that you need help, with no explanation.

2. The response
Trained staff can take you to a safe space, call a taxi, help you reach a friend, ask the other person to leave, or call security or police.

3. The catch
It only works at venues that joined and trained their staff. It began in Lincolnshire, England, in 2016 and spread to Ireland and Canada. I couldn't confirm a US program, so look for a poster first.

My niece was walked to the back office and a taxi came ten minutes later.

When she told her mother, her mother said, "I wish we'd had something like that." Many women say this.

A code word is a good idea. An even better one is a plan before the night starts.

Her advice now: look at the restroom wall for the poster when you arrive. Some venues have one, some don't. It takes ten seconds to check, and it's worth knowing before you need it.

We know how to spot a scam. Almost nobody teaches us how to spot our own body's warning signs. I put them in one place: four short books (The Belly Fat Lie, Aging Faster Than You Should, The Caffeine Trap, The 3AM Signal) and four tools. That's the Health Bundle.

cover: THE DATE ON YOUR MILK AND EGGS IS NOT A SAFETY DATE.
THE USDA SAYS "BEST BY" IS ABOUT QUALITY,
AND EXCEPT FOR INFANT FORMULA IT IS NOT REQUIRED BY LAW.
HERE'S HOW TO TELL WHAT'S ACTUALLY SAFE:

slides.text: You open the fridge. The milk says yesterday. Into the trash it goes. Most of us do this without thinking.
"Best if used by" is about quality. "Sell by" is for the store. Neither is a safety date, except on infant formula.
The FDA has estimated that confusion over date labels accounts for about 20% of food waste at home.
Smell. Look. Mold or an off smell means toss it. Properly stored food without spoilage is generally fine past the date.
I trusted a printed date over my own nose for years. What else do I trust over what my body is telling me?

cta_hook: We trust the label. Not the signal.
cta_bridge: We read every label. Nobody reads what their body is telling them.
caption:
My grandmother would have smelled the milk. I read the date and threw it out.

Last month I threw out a half gallon, a carton of eggs and a yogurt in one week. All of it was "expired" by one day. I got curious and looked up what the dates actually mean.

Here's what the USDA says, in plain words.

1. Dates aren't safety dates
Except for infant formula, the dates on food are not required by federal law and are not a safety deadline. "Best if used by" means quality. "Sell by" means the store should move it.

2. Spoilage is what matters
Properly stored food that shows no spoilage is generally safe past the date. Mold, a sour smell or a changed texture means toss it.

3. The cost
The FDA has estimated that confusion about these dates accounts for about 20% of consumer food waste.

I told my husband I'd been throwing out $20 of groceries a week for years. He laughed, then did the math.

When I mentioned it to my sister, she said, "I'd never trust my nose." But our grandmothers did, every day of their lives.

I started trusting my senses in the kitchen. It made me wonder what else I'd stopped trusting.

My neighbor, a retired nurse, told me she keeps one rule: look, smell, then decide. She hasn't had a bad stomach from the fridge in twenty years. Her fridge, she says, is mostly honest.

We check labels, bills and fine print. I started reading what my body had been trying to tell me, and put it in one place: four short books (The Belly Fat Lie, Aging Faster Than You Should, The Caffeine Trap, The 3AM Signal) and four tools. That's the Health Bundle.
